article_title: High School GPAs and ACT Scores as Predictors of College Completion
citation: Allensworth, E. (2020). High school GPAs and ACT scores as predictors of college graduation. Educational Researcher, 49(3), 198-211. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: Students' efforts to improve HSGPAs have considerable potential leverage for college readiness, unlike efforts to improve ACT scores
description: The article recommends that because HSGPAs relate strongly and consistently to college graduation while ACT signal largely reflects school factors, "students’ efforts to improve their HSGPAs would seem to have considerable potential leverage for improving college readiness." It contrasts this with little evidence that improving ACT scores raises college success.
requirements: Applies where HSGPA reflects sustained effort and skills across many classes, as the article describes
constraints: The article states there is "little evidence that students will have more college success if they work to improve their ACT score"
target_learners: High school students preparing for college
examples: The study compared graduation rates of students with the same HSGPA or ACT score across high schools
key_sources: Allensworth, E. (2020). High school GPAs and ACT scores as predictors of college graduation. Educational Researcher, 49(3), 198-211. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-GPAs-and-ACT-scores-as-predictors-of-college-completion-er-article

article_title: High School GPAs and ACT Scores as Predictors of College Completion
citation: Allensworth, E. (2020). High school GPAs and ACT scores as predictors of college graduation. Educational Researcher, 49(3), 198-211. https://journals.sagepub.com
title: HSGPA breadth theory: GPAs' multi-criteria composition makes them strong college-readiness indicators
description: The article proposes an explanatory account of why HSGPAs predict college success despite perceived inconsistency across schools. HSGPAs aggregate "effort over an entire semester in many different types of classes, demonstration of skills through multiple formats, and different teacher expectations." The authors argue this variety "might help to make HSGPAs strong indicators of readiness because they measure a very wide variety of the skills and behaviors that are needed for success in college," where students face widely varying content and expectations.
requirements: HSGPAs must draw on many criteria across different class types and formats, as the article describes
constraints: HSGPAs are perceived to represent inconsistent levels of readiness across high schools, an assumption the study tests
key_sources: Allensworth, E. (2020). High school GPAs and ACT scores as predictors of college graduation. Educational Researcher, 49(3), 198-211. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-GPAs-and-ACT-scores-as-predictors-of-college-completion-er-article

article_title: Are GPAs an Inconsistent Measure of Achievement across High Schools? Examining Assumptions about Grades versus Standardized Test Scores
citation: Allensworth, Elaine M., & Clark, Kallie. (2019). Are GPAs an Inconsistent Measure of College Readiness across High Schools? Examining Assumptions about Grades versus Standardized Test Scores. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Use high school grades, not individual test scores, as the primary formative indicator of college readiness, and rely less heavily on standardized test scores in accountability
description: The article concludes that HSGPAs "perform in a strong and consistent way across high schools as measures of college readiness, while ACT scores do not", and recommends that schools use grades formatively to guide improvement and assess college-readiness programs, while relying much less heavily on test scores. Because individual ACT scores add little beyond HSGPA and vary inconsistently across schools, districts should also track students' actual college performance rather than proxy readiness with test scores alone.
requirements: Longitudinal data systems that allow districts to track students' actual performance in college
constraints: The study used only Chicago Public Schools data and public schools; relationships could differ with a more comprehensive sample
HSGPA is not an equivalent measure of readiness across schools; school effects remain
target_learners: High school graduates enrolling in four-year colleges
target_learning_goals: Academic readiness for college persistence and graduation
examples: The authors recommend that states and districts rely less heavily on standardized test scores in accountability systems and that schools measure and publish school effects on postsecondary outcomes
key_sources: Allensworth, Elaine M., & Clark, Kallie. (2019). Are GPAs an Inconsistent Measure of College Readiness across High Schools? Examining Assumptions about Grades versus Standardized Test Scores. University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/are-gpas-inconsistent-measure-achievement-across-high-schools-examining-assumptions

article_title: Compared to What? Estimating Causal Effects for Latent Subgroups to Understand Variation in the Impacts of Head Start by Alternate Child Care Setting
citation: Avi Feller, Todd Grindal, Luke Miratrix, Lindsay C. Page. (2014). Compared to what? Estimating Causal Effects for Latent Subgroups to Understand Variation in the Impacts of Head Start by Alternate Child Care Setting. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Head Start Impact Study (HSIS) secondary dataset
description: The HSIS is the first randomized trial of Head Start in the program's history, used here as secondary data. In total, 4,440 children in 202 center groups were randomized to treatment or control; the sample was diverse (30% Black, 38% Hispanic, 30% non-English home language, 50% male). Outcomes include PPVT and Woodcock-Johnson III assessments gathered for several years after randomization.
requirements: Access to the HSIS secondary data with baseline covariates and follow-up assessments
constraints: More than one-third of control children enrolled in some form of early childhood education, complicating conventional analyses
target_learners: low-income children aged 3 and 4 in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: evaluating effects of Head Start offers on cognitive outcomes
examples: Table 1 reports percent of HSIS children by care type for 3- and 4-year-olds, treated and control
key_sources: Avi Feller, Todd Grindal, Luke Miratrix, Lindsay C. Page. (2014). Compared to what? Estimating Causal Effects for Latent Subgroups to Understand Variation in the Impacts of Head Start by Alternate Child Care Setting. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562722

article_title: Hallé SHINE on Manchester: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Victoria Menzies, Adetayo Kasim, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Nasima Akhter, Clare Collyer, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2016). Hallé SHINE on Manchester: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Music-themed Saturday school curriculum with enrichment, project work, and collaborative learning
description: The HSoM curriculum pattern organises literacy and numeracy lessons around termly musical themes, supplemented by enrichment visits and project work. SHINE's guiding principles in the 'Making it Work' handbook include "project work, hands-on learning, and opportunities for enrichment which enabled students to apply their learning to real world contexts" and "an emphasis on investigative and collaborative learning and research projects which encouraged problem-solving and independent learning". The pattern also allows curriculum flexibility for trips and visits to re-engage demotivated learners.
requirements: A musical theme set by the Hallé each term, a core focus on literacy and numeracy, and a medium-term plan per term linking learning across Saturdays
constraints: Designed for pupils who were demotivated or struggling with weekday schooling; delivered outside school hours
target_learners: Key Stage 2 pupils in host and partner primary schools
examples: Each project planned educational visits such as a trip to the space centre as part of 'The Planets' theme
key_sources: Victoria Menzies, Adetayo Kasim, Dimitra Kokotsaki, Catherine Hewitt, Nasima Akhter, Clare Collyer, Kirsty Younger, Andy Wiggins and Carole Torgerson. (2016). Hallé SHINE on Manchester: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED581134

article_title: The Role of Online Learning in Radiographic Diagnosis in Dental Education
citation: Ariel Tsao, Sang E. Park. (2016). The Role of Online Learning in Radiographic Diagnosis in Dental Education. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i3.1387
title: HSDM pilot online radiographic caries diagnosis module
description: A pilot five-module online learning program created at Harvard School of Dental Medicine for radiographic caries diagnosis, built from learning objectives of lectures given by HSDM faculty with interactive lessons including matching and multiple-choice questions. It was uploaded to cloud storage and made available to the Class of 2016 (n=31) for practice on computers or tablets at any point in time, with concepts confirmed by faculty. The module was assessed with three clinical FMX cases and a perception survey.
requirements: Concepts were confirmed by faculty before implementation
constraints: Commercial options for radiographic caries diagnosis e-learning were not available and the scope was very limited, per the article
target_learning_goals: radiographic interproximal caries diagnosis and severity classification
examples: Students completed three cases (David, Katherine, Michael) individually and in teams, with responses categorized into five classes from very over-diagnosed to very under-diagnosed
key_sources: Ariel Tsao, Sang E. Park. (2016). The Role of Online Learning in Radiographic Diagnosis in Dental Education. Journal of Education and Training Studies. https://doi.org/10.11114/jets.v4i3.1387

article_title: Development and psychometric validation of the hospital Security Personnel Narrative Competency Scale (HSPNCS).
citation: Fang Binru, Guo Lina, Zhang Hao, Yang Yongting, Wu Rong, Wu Jin, Jiang Shunjie, Zhu Liming. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of the hospital Security Personnel Narrative Competency Scale (HSPNCS). BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-15542-7
title: HSPNCS: a 36-item narrative competency scale for hospital security personnel
description: The HSPNCS is a newly developed instrument measuring narrative competency in hospital security staff. It uses a Likert 5-point scale from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). The article states: "The HSPNCS is a newly developed 36-item scale consisting of nine first-order subdomains nested within three higher-order dimensions: self-reflection, empathy, and professionalism." It is intended for assessing competency and identifying training needs.
requirements: Respondents rate items on a 5-point Likert scale from strongly disagree to strongly agree
constraints: Validated only among hospital security personnel in Zhejiang Province, China
key_sources: Fang Binru, Guo Lina, Zhang Hao, Yang Yongting, Wu Rong, Wu Jin, Jiang Shunjie, Zhu Liming. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of the hospital Security Personnel Narrative Competency Scale (HSPNCS). BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-15542-7

article_title: Development and psychometric validation of the hospital Security Personnel Narrative Competency Scale (HSPNCS).
citation: Fang Binru, Guo Lina, Zhang Hao, Yang Yongting, Wu Rong, Wu Jin, Jiang Shunjie, Zhu Liming. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of the hospital Security Personnel Narrative Competency Scale (HSPNCS). BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-15542-7
title: Three-dimension framework of narrative competency: self-reflection, empathy, professionalism
description: The article proposes a theory-driven framework extending narrative medicine to non-clinical staff. It states: "the preliminary framework of the HSPNCS comprised three higher-order dimensions: self-reflection, empathy, and professionalism." Self-reflection covers introspective processing, empathy covers listening and perspective-taking, and professionalism covers occupational identity and value. Professionalism was added as a context-specific extension beyond the classical narrative medicine definition.
requirements: Items must be adapted to the work context and educational levels of security personnel
constraints: Professionalism is a context-specific extension rather than a direct component of the classical narrative medicine definition
key_sources: Fang Binru, Guo Lina, Zhang Hao, Yang Yongting, Wu Rong, Wu Jin, Jiang Shunjie, Zhu Liming. (2026). Development and psychometric validation of the hospital Security Personnel Narrative Competency Scale (HSPNCS). BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-026-15542-7

article_title: Effects of standards of best practice in simulation-based training among midwifery students in China.
citation: Tu Lewei, Wu Huijie, Xia Xinyi, Zhu Xuehua, Mei Binbin, Zhang Yan, Xu Mengyan, Yang Yeqin. (2026). Effects of standards of best practice in simulation-based training among midwifery students in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08081-y
title: Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice (HSSOBP) as a design framework for simulation-based education
description: The INACSL Healthcare Simulation Standards of Best Practice, first established in 2009 and updated in 2021, organize simulation-based education into eleven aspects including pre-briefing, simulation design, facilitation, debriefing, and evaluation of learning & performance. The article describes them as "a comprehensive framework that guides the design, facilitation, debriefing, and evaluation of simulation activities", emphasizing a structured approach in which each phase from pre-briefing to outcomes assessment is systematically addressed. In this study the framework structured a 12-hour obstetric simulation intervention for midwifery students.
requirements: The article states simulation activities must be designed to achieve specific, shared objectives guiding the whole process, with needs assessment, SMART objectives, scenario development, pre-briefing, facilitation, guided feedback, and evaluation implemented as phases
constraints: The article notes implementation may require more nuanced approaches to enhance aspects such as support and collaboration, which showed no measurable gains
target_learners: nursing and healthcare students in simulation-based training
target_learning_goals: clinical skills and obstetric emergency management
professional knowledge, skills and attitudes in simulation
examples: The teaching team used the standards to build four high-fidelity obstetric scenarios (normal vaginal delivery, postpartum hemorrhage, pregnancy-induced hypertension, abnormal labor) in a 12-hour Comprehensive Midwifery Skills course.
key_sources: Tu Lewei, Wu Huijie, Xia Xinyi, Zhu Xuehua, Mei Binbin, Zhang Yan, Xu Mengyan, Yang Yeqin. (2026). Effects of standards of best practice in simulation-based training among midwifery students in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08081-y

article_title: Effects of standards of best practice in simulation-based training among midwifery students in China.
citation: Tu Lewei, Wu Huijie, Xia Xinyi, Zhu Xuehua, Mei Binbin, Zhang Yan, Xu Mengyan, Yang Yeqin. (2026). Effects of standards of best practice in simulation-based training among midwifery students in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08081-y
title: Standards-based simulation design sequence: needs assessment, SMART objectives, authentic scenarios, and standardized pre-briefing
description: This is the design sequence the article's intervention followed under the HSSOBP: a needs assessment aligned to training goals and clinical requirements, construction of objectives integrating needs assessment with learners' competence levels, scenario development from real clinical cases, and standardized pre-briefing. Objectives were designed to be "Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, and Time-bound (SMART)", ensuring they guided the simulation activities and aligned with the program's broader educational goals. Scenarios replicated authentic clinical workflows while targeting essential professional knowledge and clinical skills.
requirements: A multidisciplinary teaching team (the article used one obstetrician, one midwifery expert, and two simulation instructors with at least ten years of experience and a master's degree or higher), preliminary trial runs to ascertain task feasibility, and a high-fidelity environment replicating an authentic delivery room setting
constraints: The article links the intervention's failure to improve self-confidence to this brief 12-class-hour duration and to the unchanged Support dimension of the design
target_learning_goals: integration of theory and clinical practice
examples: Four high-fidelity scenarios were embedded in 12 class hours of the Comprehensive Midwifery Skills laboratory course, with pre-briefing covering roles, objectives, confidentiality principles, and limitations.
key_sources: Tu Lewei, Wu Huijie, Xia Xinyi, Zhu Xuehua, Mei Binbin, Zhang Yan, Xu Mengyan, Yang Yeqin. (2026). Effects of standards of best practice in simulation-based training among midwifery students in China. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08081-y

article_title: Card games are effective tools to enhance foundation year health and safety inductions.
citation: Rafiq R, Matthews H, Abedalreza D, Yahya F, Jones MA. (2025). Card games are effective tools to enhance foundation year health and safety inductions. FEBS Open Bio 15(12). https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.70140
title: Three health and safety card games: Hazard Hunter, PPE Lab Gear Up and Lab Equipment Identifier
description: The article describes three card games designed for laboratory health and safety inductions: "three card games were designed with the rationale of supporting student understanding in the field of laboratory health and safety". Health and Safety Hazard Hunter is a matching game for GHS hazard symbols; PPE Lab Gear Up is a scenario-based game dressing a character in appropriate PPE; Lab Equipment Identifier is a matching pairs game for liquid-measurement equipment and its accuracy category. Students played each game for 15 minutes in groups of approximately 3–5.
requirements: Delivered within a 1-hour session in the main teaching laboratory with a 10-minute introduction and 15 minutes per game in groups of approximately 3–5
constraints: Designed for foundation year laboratory health and safety induction; outcomes may vary in different international contexts
target_learners: higher education students entering laboratory-based degrees
examples: Students drew scenario cards and dressed a character in appropriate PPE in PPE Lab Gear Up
Students matched equipment cards to definitions and categorised accuracy as high, medium or low in Lab Equipment Identifier
key_sources: Rafiq R, Matthews H, Abedalreza D, Yahya F, Jones MA. (2025). Card games are effective tools to enhance foundation year health and safety inductions. FEBS Open Bio 15(12). https://doi.org/10.1002/2211-5463.70140

article_title: Effect of Training Program on Evidence-Based Practice Competencies in Hospital Nurses in Taiwan: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Yeh M.-L., Chang B.-Y., Dai H.-D., & Chung M.-H. (2025). Effect of training program on evidence-based practice competencies in hospital nurses in Taiwan: A quasi-experimental study. The Journal of Nursing Research, 33(5), e412. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000701
title: HS-EBP questionnaire: five-domain measure of evidence-based practice competence
description: The Health Sciences-Evidence-Based Practice (HS-EBP) questionnaire assesses EBP performance and factors influencing its improvement, providing "a standardized procedure for responding to most clinical situations arising in daily practice." It encompasses "60 items in the five domains of beliefs-attitudes (BeAt, 12 items), results from scientific research (Science, 14 items), development of professional practice (Practice, 10 items), assessment of results (Assess, 12 items), and barriers-facilitators for EBP (BaFa, 12 items)," scored on a 1–10 Likert scale with higher scores indicating greater agreement. In this study the Chinese version showed Cronbach αs of .98, .97, .95, .97, and .96 for the five subscales.
requirements: Assessor administration before and after intervention; a validated language version (the Chinese version by Yeh et al.) for the target population
constraints: Barriers-facilitators scores remained below 70 posttest in both groups in this study, which the authors attribute partly to workplace environment impediments not addressed by training alone
target_learners: health science professionals, here practicing clinical nurses
target_learning_goals: measuring EBP aptitude and evaluating the effectiveness of interventions designed to improve EBP performance
examples: The study used the questionnaire with an assessor blinded to group assignment at pretest and posttest, with a 1-year follow-up by another assessor.
key_sources: Yeh M.-L., Chang B.-Y., Dai H.-D., & Chung M.-H. (2025). Effect of training program on evidence-based practice competencies in hospital nurses in Taiwan: A quasi-experimental study. The Journal of Nursing Research, 33(5), e412. https://doi.org/10.1097/jnr.0000000000000701

article_title: A Mixed Methods Study Identifying the Competencies of Health Care Simulation Technicians.
citation: Roche Adam F., Condron Claire M., Eppich Walter J., O'Connor Paul E. (2023). A Mixed Methods Study Identifying the Competencies of Health Care Simulation Technicians. Simulation in Healthcare 18(5). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000682
title: Nine-domain KSA competency framework for health care simulation technicians
description: The article presents a competency framework for the health care simulation technician (HST) role, derived from job description analysis and interviews. It states: "This analysis resulted in the identification of 9 competency domains: 3 knowledge domains (technical, clinical, and pedagogic), 4 skills domains (resourcefulness, pedagogic, team, and technical), and 2 attitudes domains (professional and 'can-do' mentality)." The framework organizes individual competencies (e.g., simulation technology knowledge, moulage, willingness to learn) under these domains and is intended to guide recruitment and professional development for HSTs.
requirements: Competencies must be elicited from both job descriptions and stakeholder interviews and grouped by consensus coding into knowledge, skill, and attitude categories
constraints: The authors note possible considerable intersimulation center variability depending on the teaching and research mission of the centers and the learner population served
target_learners: Health care simulation technicians at foundation, intermediate, and senior levels
target_learning_goals: Knowledge, skills, and attitudes required to perform the health care simulation technician role
examples: The framework was built from 18 eligible online job descriptions and 30 interviews, with competencies classified using a framework method and compared against the SimGHOSTS capabilities framework
key_sources: Roche Adam F., Condron Claire M., Eppich Walter J., O'Connor Paul E. (2023). A Mixed Methods Study Identifying the Competencies of Health Care Simulation Technicians. Simulation in Healthcare 18(5). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000682

article_title: A Mixed Methods Study Identifying the Competencies of Health Care Simulation Technicians.
citation: Roche Adam F., Condron Claire M., Eppich Walter J., O'Connor Paul E. (2023). A Mixed Methods Study Identifying the Competencies of Health Care Simulation Technicians. Simulation in Healthcare 18(5). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000682
title: Use the identified KSA competencies to support HST candidate selection and continuing professional development
description: The article argues that identifying HST competencies serves recruitment and development. It states the identification of competencies will "support the selection of candidates with the attributes that will allow them to be successful in this role and guide continuous professional development opportunities for current and future HSTs." For selection specifically, it suggests designing specific interview questions that allow applicants to disclose can-do attitudes, since these are difficult to assess in traditional interviews. The findings also support constructive alignment between the HST role and training opportunities.
requirements: Access to the nine-domain competency framework and awareness that can-do attitudes need purposefully designed interview questions to assess
constraints: The article notes only 2% of surveyed simulation center directors found adequately qualified HSTs from an application pool, and can-do competencies are difficult to assess during traditional interviews
target_learners: Health care simulation technicians and applicants to HST positions
target_learning_goals: Recruitment, training, and continuous professional development aligned to HST role competencies
examples: The authors suggest designing specific interview questions that allow the applicant to disclose the willingness-to-learn competency, and recommend aligning competencies with accreditation frameworks such as CHSOS
key_sources: Roche Adam F., Condron Claire M., Eppich Walter J., O'Connor Paul E. (2023). A Mixed Methods Study Identifying the Competencies of Health Care Simulation Technicians. Simulation in Healthcare 18(5). https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000682

article_title: Remote training in laparoscopy: a randomized trial comparing home-based self-regulated training to centralized instructor-regulated training.
citation: Sloth Sigurd Beier, Jensen Rune Dall, Seyer-Hansen Mikkel, Christensen Mette Krogh, De Win Gunter. (2021). Remote training in laparoscopy: a randomized trial comparing home-based self-regulated training to centralized instructor-regulated training. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-021-08429-7
title: Offer home-based self-regulated laparoscopic training as a feasible and effective alternative to centralized instructor-regulated training only inside a supportive instructional design
description: The article concludes that "HSRT in laparoscopy is a feasible and effective alternative to CIRT when offered inside a supportive instructional design". The supportive design combines proficiency-based training with graded goals, protected training time, instructional videos, process goals, computer-generated feedback, self-evaluation, and written feedback on submitted videos. The authors argue such scaffolding lets trainees engage in home-based training with commitment and performance improvements comparable to instructor-regulated training, while enabling distributed training and timely transfer to concurrent clinical practice.
requirements: Curricular requirements, goal setting, testing, and protected training time, which the article says are essential for assuring trainees' commitment to training
Resources for developing educational supports, including time of instructional designers, participants and assessors
constraints: The article states the scaffolding needs proper construction to optimize training outcomes, and that further research is needed on trainees' preferences and facilitators and barriers to home-based training
target_learners: First-year surgical trainees in abdominal surgery, gynecology, and urology
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and retention of basic laparoscopic psychomotor skills to proficiency standards
examples: In the trial, HSRT trainees received two paid protected working days, trained on the portable eoSim box trainer at home over six weeks, and passed proficiency criteria at rates comparable to the CIRT group
key_sources: Sloth Sigurd Beier, Jensen Rune Dall, Seyer-Hansen Mikkel, Christensen Mette Krogh, De Win Gunter. (2021). Remote training in laparoscopy: a randomized trial comparing home-based self-regulated training to centralized instructor-regulated training. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-021-08429-7

article_title: The effects of training managers on management competencies to improve their management practices and work engagement of their subordinates: A single group pre- and post-test study.
citation: Adachi H, Sekiya Y, Imamura K, Watanabe K, Kawakami N. (2020). The effects of training managers on management competencies to improve their management practices and work engagement of their subordinates: A single group pre‐ and post‐test study. J Occup Health. https://doi.org/10.1002/1348-9585.12085
title: HSE management competencies framework: four competency areas and twelve sub-competencies measured by the 66-item SMCIT
description: The UK Health and Safety Executive framework organizes manager behaviors relevant to employee well-being, health, and stress into four competency areas: "Being respectful and responsible", "Managing and communicating existing and future work", "Managing the individual within the team", and "Reasoning/managing difficult situations". It was operationalized from interviews with 216 employees, 166 line managers, and 54 HR professionals into the 66-item stress management competency indicator tool (SMCIT), whose 12 sub-competencies include integrity, managing emotions, considerate approach, proactive work management, problem-solving, participative/empowering, personally accessible, sociable, empathetic engagement, managing conflict, using organizational resources, and taking responsibility for resolving issues.
requirements: Measured via self-report (Japanese SMCIT) on five-point Likert items; Japanese version reliability reported with Cronbach's alpha of 0.915, 0.951, 0.904, and 0.921 for the four scales
constraints: Developed from qualitative research in UK workplaces; in this study applied to managers in one Japanese finance company
target_learning_goals: Management competencies for supporting the well-being, health, and stress management of subordinate workers
examples: The study used the Japanese SMCIT as both the training's self-check tool and the secondary outcome measure of manager competency
key_sources: Adachi H, Sekiya Y, Imamura K, Watanabe K, Kawakami N. (2020). The effects of training managers on management competencies to improve their management practices and work engagement of their subordinates: A single group pre‐ and post‐test study. J Occup Health. https://doi.org/10.1002/1348-9585.12085

article_title: Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics
citation: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/0711.0417
title: Helping Students Learn How To Learn: open-source physics worksheets integrated with TA development resources
description: The tutorials are worksheet-based group-learning activities in which small groups make predictions and compare lines of reasoning to build understanding of basic concepts, with teaching assistants facilitating discussion rather than lecturing. They are published so instructors can "implement similar tutorials at their own institutions", and the underlying project collected "approximately 380 hours of student tutorial groups" on video.
requirements: Teaching assistants serve as facilitators who engage students in discussions of difficult concepts rather than demonstrating problem solutions.
constraints: The analyzed videotapes came from seven groups observers identified as "watchable": consistently on-task and talking to each other frequently.
target_learners: junior and senior health and life science majors in a large algebra-based introductory physics course
target_learning_goals: basic physics concepts (Newton's third law, free-body diagrams, electrostatics) and epistemological and metacognitive learning about science
examples: The study analyzed "four hours of tutorial videotape documenting three different groups of students working on three different tutorials" (Newton's third law, free-body diagrams, electrostatics).
key_sources: Rachel E. Scherr and David Hammer. (2007). Student Behavior and Epistemological Framing: Examples from Collaborative Active-Learning Activities in Physics. Submitted to Cognition and Instruction. https://arxiv.org/abs/0712.0211
